lastPrompt: Hmmmm, I think we might be relying to much on the behavior of claude. I'm thinking I'd like to test multiple sessions without a flock and see what happens. I'm guessing, the same as if two people were…

content.text:
I think you're mostly right, and the experiment is worth doing before any more work on the hook.

## Where I agree

- **Dependence on Claude Code.** The hook design leans on `CLAUDE_PID`, which is not in the documentation, and on hook behaviour that the docs leave unstated. It worked today, but any release could change it.
- **The two-humans comparison.** Most of what goes wrong with two sessions is the same as two people working in one directory. We don't forbid that either.
- **The agent-session files.** Each session writes its own `<session-id>.jsonl`, plus a `<session-id>/` directory for subagents. This session's transcript is `2eeb9bca-....jsonl`, and the directory holds about 250 such files. Two sessions write to different files, so they don't collide.

## Where two agents differ from two humans

- **They don't know about each other.** Two people sharing a directory usually know it. An agent assumes every change in the working copy is its own, and `vc-x1 push` commits the working copy whole.
- **The review step already covers most of that.** You review the working-copy diff before every push, so a second session's stray edits would show up there. That makes the lock a convenience more than a safety device.

## What I'd expect to go wrong, and would test

1. **Mixed commits in the work-repo.** Session A pushes while B has half-finished edits, and B's edits land under A's title.
2. **Mixed transcripts in the agent-repo.** A's push commits B's partial transcript too. I expect this to be harmless, since the files only grow, but it may confuse `vc-x1 lookup`, which matches code lines to transcript windows.
3. **Two pushes at once.** jj should cope, but it may report concurrent operations or a stale working copy, and the two remote pushes can race.
4. **One session resumed in two terminals.** This is the one case where two processes append to the same transcript file, since a resume keeps the session id. We saw that in the probe. It is rare, but it is the only real threat to a transcript.
5. **The cycle record.** Two cycles cannot both be "in progress" in one file. That is a limit of our protocol, not damage.

## How to run it

Not here. I'd use a throwaway dual workspace under `/tmp` with local remotes, so nothing touches GitHub or this repo.

- **Setup:** you create it with `vc-x1 init`. I can't run it myself, because it creates the `~/.claude/projects` symlink, which my sandbox blocks. I'll work out the exact command with `--dry-run` first.
- **Sessions:** you start two sessions there and paste a short prompt I write into each. Each one edits its own file and pushes, first one after the other, then at the same moment.
- **Reading the result:** afterwards I check both repos:
  - what each commit contains;
  - whether every transcript line is still valid;
  - what jj's operation log says;
  - whether `lookup` still works.

## What it decides

- **If nothing worse than mixed commits happens:** drop the hook work. Keep the `custom.md` instruction as a cheap courtesy, or remove the lock entirely. The cycle shrinks back to documents.
- **If something actually breaks:** we know exactly what the lock has to protect, and build only that.

The cycle in flight can wait. Nothing is pushed beyond the bookmark, which sits on `main`'s commit.

The plain version: your guess is probably right that two sessions are no worse than two careless people, and the transcripts are separate files. A half-hour test in a scratch workspace will tell us whether the lock is worth anything beyond a polite warning.

Do you want me to prepare the scratch workspace command and the two prompts?

content.text:
The command and prompts are below. I dry-ran the `init` and it uses only local directories under `/tmp/vc-x1-two-sessions`, with no GitHub.

## Setup (you, plain terminal)

```
vc-x1 init /tmp/vc-x1-two-sessions/ws --repo local=/tmp/vc-x1-two-sessions
```

Then open two terminals, A and B. In each:

```
cd /tmp/vc-x1-two-sessions/ws
claude
```

There are no agent-files in that workspace, so neither session will acquaint or take a lock. They just do what the prompts say.

## Test 1: one session pushes while the other has unfinished edits

Paste into A:

```
Create a file named a.txt containing three lines: alpha one, alpha two, alpha three. Do not run any version-control command. Reply "A ready" when done.
```

Paste into B:

```
Create a file named b.txt containing three lines: beta one, beta two, beta three. Do not run any version-control command. Reply "B ready" when done.
```

When both are ready, paste into A and wait for it to finish:

```
Run exactly this one command and show me its full output, then stop: vc-x1 push main --title "test: A adds a.txt" --body "Session A's first push." --yes
```

Then paste into B:

```
Run exactly this one command and show me its full output, then stop: vc-x1 push main --title "test: B adds b.txt" --body "Session B's first push." --yes
```

## Test 2: both push at the same instant

Each command waits for the top of the next minute, so the two pushes start together. Paste both within the same minute, and not in its last ten seconds.

Paste into A:

```
Append the line "alpha four" to a.txt. Then run exactly this one command and show me its full output, then stop: sleep $((60 - $(date +%s) % 60)); vc-x1 push main --title "test: A appends" --body "Session A's timed push." --yes
```

Paste into B:

```
Append the line "beta four" to b.txt. Then run exactly this one command and show me its full output, then stop: sleep $((60 - $(date +%s) % 60)); vc-x1 push main --title "test: B appends" --body "Session B's timed push." --yes
```

## Test 3: one session resumed in two terminals

1. `/exit` both sessions.
2. In A, start `claude --continue`. In B, also start `claude --continue`. Both now resume the same session.
3. Type `say one` in A, then `say two` in B, then `say three` in A, then `say four` in B.
4. `/exit` both.

## Then tell me "done"

You don't need to copy any output. I'll read the result from `/tmp/vc-x1-two-sessions`, using read-only commands so I don't disturb it:

- **Work-repo commits:** which files each commit holds, and whether B's file landed under A's title.
- **Agent-repo commits:** which transcripts each holds, and whether the pairing trailers still match.
- **Transcripts:** whether every line of every `.jsonl` is still valid, especially the one two terminals wrote to in test 3.
- **jj's operation log:** whether it recorded concurrent operations in test 2, and whether either push failed or was retried.
- **`vc-x1 lookup`:** whether it can still trace a line of `a.txt` back to the session that wrote it.

If either session reports an error from a push, leave it as it is and carry on with the next step. A failure is a result too.

You're right, and the transcripts confirm it. I searched the agent-repo: earlier sessions ran real `vc-x1 init` commands many times, and some completed all ten steps, symlink included.

**What is different now.** It comes down to one step and one setting.

- **Only step 10 is affected.** Every other `vc-x1` command, and steps 1 to 9 of `init`, write only to places my sandbox allows: the workspace, `/tmp`, `~/.cargo` and jj's config. That is why `push`, `validate`, `sync` and the rest work without trouble. Step 10 is the only thing that writes to `~/.claude/projects`, which the sandbox mounts read-only.
- **Earlier sessions hit the same wall and went around it.** The identical "Read-only file system" error appears in six earlier transcripts. Those sessions could re-run a command outside the sandbox when it was needed. The transcripts show 88 commands run that way in total, at least one of them an `init`.
- **This session can't do that.** The option to run a command outside the sandbox is turned off in this session's configuration. I was told so at the start, and it is why I didn't retry.

So the sandbox itself is not new. The escape hatch that earlier sessions used is gone. I can't tell from here whether that came from a settings change on your side or a Claude Code update. This session runs version 2.1.296.

**The two restrictions involved,** if you want to change one:

1. **Writes to `/home/wink/.claude/projects` are denied** inside the sandbox. Allowing that path would let `init` and `vc-x1 symlink` finish from my commands.
2. **Running a command outside the sandbox is disabled.** Re-enabling it restores what earlier sessions had, with a permission prompt each time.

Both are sandbox settings, so they are yours to change, not mine. I'd lean towards the first, since it is narrower. One caveat I can't check: `~/.claude/projects` appears on a built-in protected list, so Claude Code may not let it be opened up at all.

**For the test today, neither is needed.** The workspace exists apart from the symlink. One command from your terminal finishes it:

```
cd /tmp/vc-x1-two-sessions/ws
vc-x1 symlink
```

The plain version: I can run `init`, and earlier sessions did. The only step that fails is creating the link under `~/.claude/projects`. Earlier sessions got past it by running outside the sandbox, which this session is not allowed to do.

content.text:
No, `probe.sh` stays out of it. That was a separate experiment, about hooks, and it is finished. The two-session test uses no hooks at all.

I looked at `agent-tests/xxx`, and I think the two experiments got crossed. What was run there is the probe's "run 1" (`hi`, `/clear`, `hi`, `/exit`) in both terminals, not test 1 of the two-session test.

**What I see in `xxx`:**

- **Work-repo:** only the initial commit. There is no `a.txt` or `b.txt`, and nothing was pushed.
- **Agent-repo directory:** six transcript files, three per terminal: a `hi`, a `/clear`, and a second `hi`.

**It still told us something useful.** Two sessions were open in the same workspace at the same time, and:

- each wrote only to its own files, named by session id;
- every line in all six files is valid, with no interleaving or damage;
- a `/clear` starts a new transcript file, which matches what the probe showed about session ids.

So your guess about the transcripts holds so far. What is not yet tested is the part involving pushes.

**The two-session test, test 1, again.** Start `claude` in `agent-tests/xxx` in terminals A and B.

Paste into A:

```
Create a file named a.txt containing three lines: alpha one, alpha two, alpha three. Do not run any version-control command. Reply "A ready" when done.
```

Paste into B:

```
Create a file named b.txt containing three lines: beta one, beta two, beta three. Do not run any version-control command. Reply "B ready" when done.
```

When both say ready, paste into A and wait for it to finish:

```
Run exactly this one command and show me its full output, then stop: vc-x1 push main --title "test: A adds a.txt" --body "Session A's first push." --yes
```

Then paste into B:

```
Run exactly this one command and show me its full output, then stop: vc-x1 push main --title "test: B adds b.txt" --body "Session B's first push." --yes
```

Tests 2 and 3 follow from my earlier message, unchanged. Tell me when you've done as many as you want, and I'll read the results.

content.text:
Test 1 went as predicted, with no errors and no damage. One result is worth noting beyond what we expected.

**What happened**

- **A's push took both files.** The work-repo commit `test: A adds a.txt` contains `a.txt` and `b.txt`. Session B's unfinished work went out under A's title, exactly the "two people in one directory" case.
- **B's push had nothing left to commit in the work-repo.** `vc-x1` warned: "work repo had no pending changes; the supplied message is not applied". So there is no work-repo commit titled `test: B adds b.txt`.
- **B's push still made an agent-repo commit,** titled `test: B adds b.txt`, holding the newest lines of both transcripts.
- **The transcripts are intact.** Every line of every file parses. A's agent-repo commit includes part of B's transcript, and B's includes the tail of A's. They are mixed across commits but nothing is lost or corrupted.
- **jj had no trouble.** Both pushes reported "completed all stages (verified)".

**The result I didn't predict: a one-way link**

- The work-repo commit's trailer points at A's agent-repo commit only.
- B's agent-repo commit carries a trailer pointing back at that same work commit.

So two agent-repo commits claim one work commit, and the work commit knows about only one of them. A reader starting from the code finds A's session. B's session, which actually wrote `b.txt`, is reachable only from the agent-repo side. Nothing is broken, but the record of who wrote `b.txt` is misleading: the title says A, and the link says A.

This is the situation the existing Todo entry "vc-x1 push: record uncovered work commits (N:1 work<->agent)" describes. Two sessions make it happen routinely.

**One small thing to watch.** Claude Code created a `.claude/` directory in `xxx` during the test. It holds only an empty `.cc-writes` directory so far, which git ignores. But the `.gitignore` that `init` generates has no `/.claude` line, unlike vc-x1's own. If the sandbox drops its empty placeholder files there, as it did in this repo, the next push would commit them. I'll check for that after test 2.

**Where this leaves your question.** So far the evidence supports your guess: nothing breaks, and the cost is attribution. Work lands under the wrong title, and the link to the session that wrote it is one-way. Your review of the diff before each push would catch the first. Nothing currently catches the second.

Test 2, both pushing at the same instant, is the one that could still show a real failure. The prompts are in my earlier message. Paste both within the same minute, and not in its last ten seconds.

content.text:
Test 2 produced real trouble. Nothing was lost or corrupted, but the history it left is a mess.

**What happened, in the same second (18:17:00)**

- **B's push failed partway.** It committed, pushed the work-repo, then stopped with `error: Concurrent checkout` and exit code 1. Its agent-repo stage never ran.
- **A's push reported success:** "completed all stages (verified)".
- **jj coped.** Its operation log shows "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflicts and no divergent commits.

**What the history looks like now**

| Work-repo commit | What it actually contains |
|---|---|
| `test: B appends` | both edits (A's line and B's line), plus 23 empty junk files |
| `test: A appends` | none of A's edit, only the deletion of those 23 junk files |

- **Titles don't match contents.** The commit titled "A appends" appends nothing.
- **Links are wrong.** A's push made no agent-repo commit of its own and adopted B's as its partner. Both work commits now point at the same agent-repo commit, `test: B appends`, which points back only at B's.
- **The end state is correct anyway.** Both remotes have everything, `a.txt` and `b.txt` each have four lines, the junk files are gone from the tip, and every transcript line still parses.

**The junk files are a separate finding.** They are the sandbox's placeholders: `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json` and twenty more.

- **How they got in:** each session's sandbox creates them on disk while one of its commands runs. A session doesn't see its own, but the other session's snapshot did, and committed them.
- **Why it matters beyond this test:** I'd expect the same if you run `jj st` or `vc-x1 squash-push` in your terminal at the moment an agent command is running, though I haven't tested that.
- **The gap:** vc-x1's own `.gitignore` lists these names. The `.gitignore` that `init` generates does not.

**What I make of it**

- **Your guess holds for data safety.** Two sessions lose nothing, and jj and the transcripts both survive.
- **It does not hold for the record.** One push fails with an error that explains nothing, a commit's title lies about its content, and the code-to-session links are wrong. Provenance is the thing `vc-x1` exists to get right, so this is the damage that matters.
- **It needs real simultaneity.** Test 1, a few minutes apart, had only the milder problems. Test 2 needed the same second.

**My recommendation**

1. **Keep the lock as it is today,** the instruction in `custom.md`. It is cheap and prevents exactly this.
2. **Drop the hook work.** It adds dependence on undocumented Claude Code behaviour to guard against something that is rare and now understood.
3. **Record the findings** and file two Todo entries:
   - `init` writes the sandbox's names into `.gitignore`;
   - `push` under a concurrent push adopts the wrong partner and fails without explanation.

That would shrink the cycle in flight back to documents: the findings, the two entries, and the closing.

The plain version: two sessions at once don't destroy anything, but they leave commits with wrong titles, wrong links and junk files, and one push dies confusingly. The simple lock we already have is worth keeping, and the hook is not worth building.

Test 3, one session resumed in two terminals, is still open. It only concerns whether a single transcript file survives two writers. Do you want to run it, or stop here and have me write up the findings?

cd /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/agent-tests/xxx

I'm naming the session id explicitly so both terminals are certain to be on the same session. It is the one that was terminal A's in the earlier tests.

Test 3 worked, and you were fast enough: both "count" prompts are stamped in the same second (01:34:14), so two terminals really were writing to one file at once.

**What the file shows**

- **One file, two writers, no damage.** Both terminals wrote to `b7c0c24b-....jsonl`. It has 98 lines and every one parses. Claude Code did not give either terminal a separate file.
- **All eight messages are there:** `say one` to `say four` with their replies, and both counts with theirs. The two count replies were written a second apart with nothing garbled.

# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do

The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. This file
holds what was found out about it on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's
place, and what happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's
own tests, of 2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.

The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, the instruction is kept, and
no hook is built.

## What the lock is today

- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
  touches the lock.
- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
  the instruction has it stop then.
- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.

## What a hook could do

A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.

- From the documents:
  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
    every call.
  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
- From the probe:
  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
    documents do not name that variable.
  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
    as a lock should is the process id.
- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.

## What two sessions do with no lock

Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
operation log.

- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
    commit under B's title.
  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
    deleted them.
  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
    same second, and every line of it parses.
  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.

## What was decided

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`. It costs a line and it prevents all of the
  above.
- No hook, and no code in `vc-x1` for the session lock.
- The failed push and the wrong partner are two `vc-x1` runs overlapping, which is what the lock
  `vc-x1` takes for a run is for ([vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every
  run](../TODO.md#vc-x1-takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-every-run)).
- The empty files are a fault of the `.gitignore` that `init` writes ([init writes the agent
  sandbox's names into
  .gitignore](../TODO.md#init-writes-the-agent-sandboxs-names-into-gitignore)).
- Not tested: which branch a resume of a forked transcript takes, what `vc-x1 lookup` makes of
  one, and whether a user's own `jj st` beside a running agent command picks up the sandbox's
  files as the second session's snapshot did. We think it does.

# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do

The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. This file
holds what was found out about it on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's
place, and what happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's
own tests, of 2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.

The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, the instruction is kept, and
no hook is built.

## What the lock is today

- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
  touches the lock.
- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
  the instruction has it stop then.
- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.

## What a hook could do

A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.

- From the documents:
  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
    every call.
  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
- From the probe:
  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
    documents do not name that variable.
  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
    as a lock should is the process id.
- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.

## What two sessions do with no lock

Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
operation log.

- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
    commit under B's title.
  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
    deleted them.
  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
    same second, and every line of it parses.
  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.

## What was decided

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`. It costs a line and it prevents all of the
  above.
- No hook, and no code in `vc-x1` for the session lock.
- The failed push and the wrong partner are two `vc-x1` runs overlapping, which is what the lock
  `vc-x1` takes for a run is for ([vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every
  run](../TODO.md#vc-x1-takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-every-run)).
- The empty files are a fault of the `.gitignore` that `init` writes ([init writes the agent
  sandbox's names into
  .gitignore](../TODO.md#init-writes-the-agent-sandboxs-names-into-gitignore)).
- Not tested: which branch a resume of a forked transcript takes, what `vc-x1 lookup` makes of
  one, and whether a user's own `jj st` beside a running agent command picks up the sandbox's
  files as the second session's snapshot did. We think it does.

# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do

The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. This file
holds what was found out about it on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's
place, and what happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's
own tests, of 2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.

The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, the instruction is kept, and
no hook is built.

## What the lock is today

- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
  touches the lock.
- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
  the instruction has it stop then.
- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.

## What a hook could do

A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.

- From the documents:
  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
    every call.
  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
- From the probe:
  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
    documents do not name that variable.
  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
    as a lock should is the process id.
- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.

## What two sessions do with no lock

Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
operation log.

- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
    commit under B's title.
  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
    deleted them.
  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
    same second, and every line of it parses.
  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.

## What was decided

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`. It costs a line and it prevents all of the
  above.
- No hook, and no code in `vc-x1` for the session lock.
- The failed push and the wrong partner are two `vc-x1` runs overlapping, which is what the lock
  `vc-x1` takes for a run is for ([vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every
  run](../TODO.md#vc-x1-takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-every-run)).
- The empty files are a fault of the `.gitignore` that `init` writes ([init writes the agent
  sandbox's names into
  .gitignore](../TODO.md#init-writes-the-agent-sandboxs-names-into-gitignore)).
- Not tested: which branch a resume of a forked transcript takes, what `vc-x1 lookup` makes of
  one, and whether a user's own `jj st` beside a running agent command picks up the sandbox's
  files as the second session's snapshot did. We think it does.

42	  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
43	    documents do not name that variable.
44	  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
45	  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
46	  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
47	    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
48	    as a lock should is the process id.
49	- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
50	  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
51	  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
52	- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
53	  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.
54	
55	## What two sessions do with no lock
56	
57	Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
58	with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
59	the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
60	operation log.
61	
62	- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
63	  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
64	  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
65	    commit under B's title.
66	  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
67	- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
68	  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
69	    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
70	  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
71	    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
72	  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
73	    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
74	    deleted them.
75	  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
76	    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
77	- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
78	  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
79	    same second, and every line of it parses.
80	  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
81	    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
82	- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
83	  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
84	    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
85	- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
86	  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
87	  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.
88	
89	## What was decided
90	
91	- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`. It costs a line and it prevents all of the
92	  above.
93	- No hook, and no code in `vc-x1` for the session lock.
94	- The failed push and the wrong partner are two `vc-x1` runs overlapping, which is what the lock
95	  `vc-x1` takes for a run is for ([vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every
96	  run](../TODO.md#vc-x1-takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-every-run)).
97	- The empty files are a fault of the `.gitignore` that `init` writes ([init writes the agent
98	  sandbox's names into
99	  .gitignore](../TODO.md#init-writes-the-agent-sandboxs-names-into-gitignore)).
100	- Not tested: which branch a resume of a forked transcript takes, what `vc-x1 lookup` makes of
101	  one, and whether a user's own `jj st` beside a running agent command picks up the sandbox's
102	  files as the second session's snapshot did. We think it does.
103	
</system-reminder>

Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it.

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

# AGENTS.md - Agent Instructions

The universal core of the agent instructions: the dual-repo model, the hard rules, the cycle
protocol, and a map of the rest. One of the [agent-files](#terminology), carried by every adopter.
The rules are an index: each is a sentence and a link to the section that holds it, and a
section's why is in [rationale.md](agent-data/rationale.md) under the mirrored heading.

## Terminology

Repos: the two repos of [the dual-repo model](#the-dual-repo-model), "work-repo" and "agent-repo",
always hyphenated.

Agent-files: the instruction set an agent reads: `AGENTS.md`, `custom.md`, `agent-data/*`, and
anything `custom.md` points at. `TODO.md` is not one, since its content is the project's record,
but the agent-files require that there is one, of the shape in [Todo
format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format).

Agent-files version: the set's own version, `vX.Y.Z`, the name of an empty
`agent-data/agent-files-vX.Y.Z` file, bumped by `agent-files` proposal cycles and copied by
adoptions ([Agent-files version](agent-data/versioning.md#agent-files-version)).

Project layer: the project's own agent-files, `custom.md` and what it points at.

Set: the agent-files as the template repository's payload carries them, the copy every adopter
starts from and re-syncs to. Adopter: a project carrying a copy of the set. Maintainer: whoever
owns the template repository and decides what the payload takes.

Cycle: one change, run from opening to closing as one commit or a ladder of them, each made by
`vc-x1 push` ([Cycle protocol](#cycle-protocol)). Single-step when the problem statement has one
straightforward solution step, its documentation in the same commit, otherwise multi-step. Both run
on a bookmark under the dev name, and the shape is fixed at the cycle's first push ([Cycle
shape](#cycle-shape)).

Land: the sequence that makes a cycle permanent, on the user's go at the close-out
([Land](agent-data/jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)). Before it the cycle is a draft on its
bookmark, after it the commits are permanent.

Trapezoid: the default close-out shape, a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk line and
whose second is the cycle's ladder ([Close-out shapes](agent-data/jj.md#close-out-shapes)). Names
both the merge commit and the figure the graph draws around it.

Artifact: the work-repo's built product. It carries a `-dev` name while a cycle runs ([Dev artifact
name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)) and is installed at Land.

Rationale: a rule's why, in [rationale.md](agent-data/rationale.md) under the heading that mirrors
the rule's, reached by `[why](agent-data/rationale.md#<same-slug>)`. Read when changing a rule,
not when following one.

## The dual-repo model

Two separate jj-git colocated repos ([jj.md](agent-data/jj.md)), located by a `.vc-config.md`,
never by the current directory ([.vc-config.md](agent-data/jj.md#vc-configmd),
[why](agent-data/rationale.md#the-dual-repo-model)):

1. Work-repo: the project's work product. Its directory is the workspace root, the directory
   holding the work-repo's `.vc-config.md`, whose `[repos] work` is `"."`.
2. Agent-repo: the agent's session data, in the directory that file's `[repos] agent` names, a
   path relative to the workspace root or an absolute one, so it may sit anywhere. Written
   `<agent-dir>` wherever a command below needs it, and reached by Claude Code through a symlink
   at `~/.claude/projects/<mangled-project-path>`, which `vc-x1 init` creates for a dual
   workspace and `vc-x1 symlink` creates on demand.

## Rules

The rules, indexed: each a one-sentence summary and a link to the section that states it, this
file's rules first and then the outer files' in their order ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#rules)).
The section is the rule, the sentence its handle. None is absolute: a rule bends only when the
user says so explicitly, at the moment or as a scoped delegation ([Stop and ask](#stop-and-ask) is
the path), and the exception is recorded in the cycle's records, naming what the bend covers and
what it does not, so a waiver over a cycle's pushes says whether Land is inside it. No rule bends
silently.

- Read custom.md first: read [custom.md](custom.md), whose rules override all others.
- Acquaint before work: a session acquaints first, and what its repo check finds is reported and
  left as found until the user says how to proceed ([Acquaint](#acquaint)).
- A session's rules are its own agent-files: the ones it started in, binding in every repo it
  writes, and another repo's rules bind only by delegation ([A session's rules are its own
  agent-files](#a-sessions-rules-are-its-own-agent-files)).
- Bookmark per cycle: a cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work-repo, and `main` advances
  only when the cycle lands ([Cycles run on a bookmark](#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)).
- Shape at the first push: single-step or multi-step is fixed by the cycle's first push, and a
  ladder lands as a trapezoid or kept separate, never squashed ([Cycle shape](#cycle-shape)).
- Read the step before the action: [The per-rung flow](#the-per-rung-flow) before commit work,
  [Before any push](#before-any-push) before a push, from the file, not from memory.
- Push commits: a cycle rung is committed only by `vc-x1 push` ([Committing vs
  pushing](#committing-vs-pushing)).
- Approval per push: every push needs the user's explicit approval, or an explicit waiver
  ([Before any push](#before-any-push)).
- Hard stop after the final push: after the turn's final push nothing until the user speaks,
  unless an explicit waiver ([At rest](#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)).
- Stop and ask: on ambiguous input, on any deviation from the agreed plan, and when 5+ minutes
  on a simple task has produced no progress ([Stop and ask](#stop-and-ask)).
- Changing the agent-files: an agent-file change is its own commit and convention work its own
  cycle, and intent picks the file, the set's copy for the set, `custom.md` for this project
  only ([Changing the agent-files](#changing-the-agent-files)).
- jj, not git: version-control operations use jj ([jj basics](agent-data/jj.md#jj-basics)).
- No hand-written trailers: `vc-x1 push` stamps `ochid:` trailers, never write one by hand
  ([ochid trailers](agent-data/jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)).
- No re-describe without coordinating: never `jj describe` a published or trailer-carrying
  commit ([Re-describing](agent-data/jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)).
- Prose style: durable text is in the prose form, typeable punctuation included ([Prose
  form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form)).
- One title per step: the ladder rung and the commit title are verbatim identical
  ([Conventional-commit shape](agent-data/prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit)).
- Alert on unwrap: say so when introducing an `unwrap` / `expect` / `unwrap_or*` site, with its
  `// OK: ...` comment ([`// OK` comments](agent-data/code.md#-ok--comments-on-unwrap-calls-rust)).

## Acquaint

What a session does first, at its start and whenever the user says "acquaint" or "reacquaint",
in this order ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#acquaint)):

1. custom.md: read [custom.md](custom.md), and do what it asks for at acquaint.
2. Repo check: look at each repo of the workspace for the four findings below, and report what is
   found before anything else. Nothing is opened, pushed, rebased, committed, or discarded until
   the user says how to proceed.
   - Not level: fetch, `jj git fetch -R .` and `jj git fetch -R <agent-dir>`, and compare `main`
     with the remote's, as `jj bookmark list --all-remotes` prints them, and the cycle's bookmark
     likewise when one is in flight. Behind, ahead, and diverged are each a finding, and a fetch
     that fails is reported as the check not made.
   - Uncommitted work: a work-repo `@` that is not empty, as `jj st` prints it. What the
     continuation notes account for, the notes themselves or a rung in flight they describe, is
     theirs to direct at step 3, and any other change is a finding. The agent-repo's `@` holds the
     session's own data and is never one.
   - Work off `main`: commits on a bookmark, a cycle's or any other, that do not descend from the
     remote's `main`. The user is told, and a rebase onto `main` is suggested.
   - Conflicts: a conflicted commit or working copy, as `jj st` and `jj log -r 'conflicts()'` show
     them. The acquaint stops there and the user is informed.
3. TODO.md: read the acquaint slice ([File
   reads](agent-data/notes.md#file-reads-read-the-slice-you-need)), the continuation notes first,
   each acted on, filed or kept, and the section reset ([Todo
   format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format)).
4. Report: say where things stand, the cycle in flight or the top of `## Todo`, and wait.

## Cycle protocol

How a [cycle](#terminology) runs ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycle-protocol)). Its record is
`TODO.md > ## In Progress` and nothing else ([Cycle-record](#cycle-record)). The `.vc-config.md`
`[validate]` table defines the commands that validate the work-repo.

### Cycles run on a bookmark

A cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work-repo, created at the opening and named by the cycle
title's slug ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). `main` advances only when
the finished cycle lands on it, so development is never done on `main`, a single-step cycle
included. The agent-repo needs no bookmark. Commands in [Cycle
bookmarks](agent-data/jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), the long-lived case in [Long-lived
bookmarks][llb].

### Cycle shape

Single-step or multi-step is decided at the opening and fixed by the cycle's first push, with the
one coordinated exception below ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycle-shape)). Before that push the
In Progress block may be rewritten to either shape. After it:

- A single-step cycle is one commit, made by one push, carrying the opening's duties, the work, and
  the close-out's duties, titled with the bare cycle title in both repos. When the work turns out to
  need more steps, two choices, since the bookmark is still a draft:
  - land the commit as it is and run the additional work as one or more further cycles
  - turn the commit into the opening: amend its version-of-record to the `-0` form, re-title it with
    " opening" as a coordinated re-describe that keeps the `ochid:` trailer ([No re-describe without
    coordinating](agent-data/jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)), and
    complete the cycle as multi-step.
- A multi-step cycle is a ladder and lands as a trapezoid or kept separate, never squashed: every
  rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, and a squash discards all but one. A ladder that shrinks
  to one rung still closes as a ladder, since its opening already pushed.

### Unplanned work

Work that arrives while a cycle runs goes one of two ways, and the user picks which
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#unplanned-work)):

- A rung inserted into the ladder, usually when it is inside the cycle's subject or blocks it.
- A `## Todo` or `## Waiting` entry, run as its own cycle later.

A rung inserted while the working copy already holds the next rung's edits sets those edits aside
as a patch first, so the inserted rung's commit carries its own change alone, and they return once
it has pushed.

### Cycle-record

A cycle's record is its `TODO.md > ## In Progress` block and nothing else, the cycle-record
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycle-record)).

- Items: title, problem, solution, acceptance check, deliberation, and the ladder heading its rung
  subsections, all provisional until close-out ([The In Progress
  block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block)).
- Life: written at the opening, revised as rungs land, finalized by the closing commit, which moves
  it whole to `## Closed` (a single-step cycle's one commit writes it there directly), deleted by
  the next opening.
  - `## In Progress` reads `_No cycle currently in progress._` between cycles.
  - The closing commit's tree carries the final form, and the file never grows.
- After that jj holds it: `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` finds the commits, on the title the
  pushed bookends carry when a rename came mid-cycle, and the landmark on `main` (the trapezoid
  merge, or the single-step commit) holds the finished block in its `TODO.md > ## Closed`.
- No backfill: a rung carries no `[[N]]` placeholder, no SHA, and no version.
- Never amended: a late finding about a closed cycle is recorded where it is found, citing the
  landmark.
- Design findings that must outlive the cycle go into a `notes/` file by the rung that made them,
  never left in the block.
- Frozen history: `notes/chores/` and `notes/done.md` are never appended, still linked.

### Opening

The cycle's first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle starts at its first commit, which
then carries step 1). A single-step cycle does all of it in its one commit, after step 1 ([Cycle
shape](#cycle-shape)). Before that commit ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#opening)):

1. Bookmark: create and publish the cycle's bookmark, a push that needs approval.
2. Waiting: check each `## Waiting` entry's condition, and promote what is met into `## Todo` at
   the rank it names.
3. In Progress block: delete whatever `## Closed` holds, then move the chosen `## Todo` entry into
   `## In Progress`, shaped as [The In Progress block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block)
   says, the specimen in [cycle-model.md](agent-data/cycle-model.md).
4. Bump: bump the version-of-record to the opening's version ([Suffix
   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), and the agent-files version with it when the
   cycle is an `agent-files` proposal ([Agent-files
   version](agent-data/versioning.md#agent-files-version)).
5. Rename: when the built artifact has consumers, rename `<name>` to `<name>-dev` ([Dev artifact
   name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)). Land restores it.

Rungs are named, not numbered ([Steps are named, not numbered][snn]), and a multi-step cycle's
bookends are the cycle title plus " opening" and " closing" ([Cycle bookend titles][cbt]).

### The per-rung flow

Every commit (opening, each rung between, closing) goes through these steps, read from here
immediately before acting ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#the-per-rung-flow)):

1. Mark current: mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Bump: bump the version-of-record to this commit's version ([Suffix
   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), the agent-files version beside it in an
   `agent-files` proposal cycle.
3. Work: do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop ([Stop and
   ask](#stop-and-ask)).
4. Rung subsection: write what this rung changed, conceptually, into its subsection under the
   ladder. The rung stays `(current)` until step 7.
5. Validate: `vc-x1 validate` before every review, doc-only commits included. The full run rewrites
   files (`cargo fmt`), so use `--fast` while a review iterates.
6. Work review: stop before writing any description and say "please review", as its own message with
   no title or body. Iterate until the user says "continue" / "go". The review is of the
   working-copy diff ([jj basics](agent-data/jj.md#jj-basics)).
7. Flip and describe: flip `(current)` to `(done)` the moment "done" is true, then write the
   description in [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form), read from the file first
   with its specimen, [commit-model.md](agent-data/commit-model.md) ([Commit
   description](#commit-description)).
8. Description review: show the title + body and stop. Ask permission to commit and push without
   spelling out the invocation. The go covers the push only when it says so.
9. Commit + push: on the go, `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."` ([Committing vs
   pushing](#committing-vs-pushing)), then [At rest](#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push).

### Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`, never pre-committed with `jj commit`
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#committing-vs-pushing)). "Commit", "push",
and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit` is asked for by name and is for local
saves and [local ladder](#local-ladders) intermediates. What push does is in [vc-x1 push][vpush].

### Commit description

The title is a Conventional Commit, distinct within its cycle ([Commit titles and
descriptions][cdd]).
The body is in [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form): no version, file list, or
deliberation ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#commit-description)).

### Pushing

Pushing is by `vc-x1 push`. The bookmark moves (create, land, trapezoid) use `jj git push` as jj.md
names, until vc-x1 owns them.

#### Before any push

([why](agent-data/rationale.md#before-any-push))

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval, or an explicit waiver covers it.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are written. Nothing follows the turn's final push.

#### At rest: push, stop, squash-push

The contract that keeps both repos clean, the rule **Hard stop after the final push** its first
item's tail ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. The agent publishes: completing a step means issuing its publishing command. The agent says what
   is worth saying *before* the final publishing command, responds with the one word "Published",
   and does nothing further until the user speaks.
2. The user squash-pushes: `vc-x1 squash-push -R <agent-dir>` whenever they want both repos fully
   pushed.

"Clean" means both repos' `@` empty. A late work-repo tweak after the push is a remote rewrite and
takes approval like any push ([vc-x1 push][vpush]).

### Close-out

The cycle's last commit is bookkeeping and its body describes that bookkeeping. A single-step cycle
does all of it in its one commit, step 5 aside ([Cycle shape](#cycle-shape)):

1. Acceptance check: run the check the opening stated and record pass or fail. A failure is a
   finding, and why it failed is determined.
2. Finalize the cycle-record in place ([Cycle-record](#cycle-record)):
   - sync the title if the scope shifted, and every anchor back-reference with it. A pushed rung
     title and the bookend pair keep their names, since retitling one is a re-describe of a
     published commit, so a rename mid-cycle reaches the block's text and the unpushed rungs only
   - replace the provisional solution statement with what was done
   - add the design subsections the deliberation grew
   - complete the closing rung's subsection
   - ask what in the block must outlive the cycle, and write it into the `notes/` file it
     belongs to
   - move the block whole to `## Closed`, leaving `## In Progress` reading
     `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
3. Validate: full validation, and update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
4. Size: when an agent-file changed, record the line count in `notes/agent-files-size.md`,
   smaller being the quasi-goal. A cycle that touched none adds no row.
5. Close-out shape ([Close-out shapes](agent-data/jj.md#close-out-shapes)):
   - choose with the user: trapezoid (the default) or keep separate
   - record the choice in the closing rung's subsection
   - reshape nothing yet, Land does.
6. Land: on the user's go, restore the plain name, reshape per the choice, fast-forward `main`,
   install the artifact, delete the bookmark locally and remotely ([Bookmark per
   cycle](#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark), [Land](agent-data/jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
7. Restart: the user restarts the agent, and before the exit anything the next agent needs is
   written into `TODO.md > ## Continuation notes`, the first section, which the next acquaint reads
   first, files or keeps, and resets ([Todo format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format)).

### Local ladders

A rung that wants incremental review runs as a local ladder: a chain of jj commits that never leaves
the machine and collapses into the rung before the cycle continues, each validated with
`vc-x1 validate --fast` ([Local ladders](agent-data/jj.md#local-ladders),
[why](agent-data/rationale.md#local-ladders)).

[cbt]: agent-data/prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit
[cdd]: agent-data/prose.md#commit-titles-and-descriptions
[llb]: agent-data/jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged
[snn]: agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered
[vpush]: agent-data/jj.md#vc-x1-push-what-it-does-and-does-not-do

## Working practices

([why](agent-data/rationale.md#working-practices))

- One command per invocation: no bundled steps (`a && b; c`), except a genuine pipeline or a tight
  pair where the join is the point.
- Exit status: never mask a command's exit status. No piping a validating command into `tail` /
  `grep` (`${PIPESTATUS[0]}` when a pipe is wanted), no `&&` after a piped stage, no trailing
  `; echo "exit=$?"`. To report and still fail: `cmd || { rc=$?; echo failed=$rc; exit $rc; }`.
- Scratch files: repo-local `tmp/` (gitignored, `mkdir -p tmp` on demand). `/tmp` is for
  out-of-project temporaries.
- Slice reads: read the slice you need from long notes files. The acquaint read is `TODO.md`
  `offset=0, limit=60` ([notes.md](agent-data/notes.md#file-reads-read-the-slice-you-need)).
- https remotes: use https remotes, and check for an ssh remote first when a push dies at the
  network leg. A remote URL change needs the user's go.
- Delegate: mechanical subtasks go to lesser models (Opus/Haiku/Sonnet).
- No memory directory: `~/.claude/projects/<path>/memory/` is unused, the agent-files are.
- Speculation: mark it in durable text with "We think ..." ([Speculation
  marker](agent-data/prose.md#speculation-marker)).
- Plain synopsis: end a technical explanation in conversation with one, marked "The plain version:"
  ([Plain synopsis](agent-data/prose.md#plain-synopsis-after-technical-explanations)).

### A session's rules are its own agent-files

A session's rules are the agent-files of the project it started in, and rules living in any other
repo are ignored unless these files or the user direct otherwise
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#a-sessions-rules-are-its-own-agent-files)). So another repo's own
protocol (a shared store's README, another project's agent-files) governs a write to it only as
far as the delegation reaches, and this file's conduct rules, the step reads, the reviews, the
per-push approval, and the stops, bind every commit and push the session makes, in any repo,
cycle or not. A repo with a live agent of its own is not written at all: message its agent.

### Stop and ask

Stop and ask on ambiguous input, on any deviation from the agreed plan, and when 5+ minutes on a
simple task has produced no progress ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#stop-and-ask)).

## Changing the agent-files

The official copies are the template repository's payload, and every adopter carries its own
copy ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#changing-the-agent-files)).

- Payload read-only: only a *correction* (a factual error, a typo, a stale cross-reference) goes
  straight in.
- Intent picks the file: a rule change meant for the set goes into the local copy of the agent-file
  it lives in, reviewed at convergence on the diff. One meant for this project only goes to
  `custom.md` and says why.
- Diff is the proposal: the diff between an adopter and the payload *is* its open proposal set.
- Own commit, own cycle: an agent-file change is its own commit, and convention work is its own
  cycle. A convention itch mid-feature becomes a backlog entry, never an inserted rung.
- Local experiments: a local agent-file may hold an unagreed experiment. Diff against the payload
  when that matters.
- Convergence: the maintainer reviews the adopters' diffs, folds what it accepts into the payload,
  and every adopter re-syncs.
- Retirement: a resolved experiment retires like a finished Todo, adopted and rejected alike: the
  cycle that resolved it is its record.
- Adopted ahead: a rule adopted ahead of its convention cycle lives in the agent-file it belongs
  to, never in a holding section of the project layer.

## custom.md

[custom.md](custom.md) is the project's own layer and is never universal
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#custommd)). It ships holding only its own shape, and a project adds
what it needs. Anyone may change any agent-file. custom.md is provided so an adopter can experiment
with, or override, a rule in one file when that is practical, and keep its other agent-files
identical to the payload's, so a re-sync is a copy:

- Overriding: a rule the adopter cannot keep as written goes under `## Project conventions and
  overrides`, naming the section it supersedes.
- Editing instead: an adopter with reasons custom.md cannot serve edits the agent-files directly,
  and its diff from the payload is its proposal ([Changing the
  agent-files](#changing-the-agent-files)). Defining what the set itself is, as its first adopters
  are doing, is one such reason. Such an adopter's custom.md holds pointers to project files and
  nothing else, and `## Project conventions and overrides` stays `_None._`.
- Pointer entries: an entry that only points at a further file owes no justification, and an
  agent-file asking for something "in custom.md" is answered by following the pointer.
- Precedence: custom.md is loaded last and wins conflicts with the other agent-files.

# Memory

This project keeps durable agent context in its agent-files, `AGENTS.md` at the work-repo root and
what it links, which are committed, diffed, and reviewable. The per-project memory directory is
intentionally empty, as `AGENTS.md > Working practices` says under "No memory directory".
